title: Multimeter basics and checking a power supply
description: Use a multimeter safely to measure DC voltage and continuity, and check that a PSU's outputs are within tolerance.
objectives: Set up a multimeter for DC voltage and continuity.
Measure a CMOS battery and judge whether it needs replacing.
Read a PSU tester and know the ATX voltage tolerances.
Identify PSU wire colours by voltage.
tools: A known-good network or power cable for continuity practice

safety.text: Never measure mains (220 V AC) wall sockets or anything inside a power supply as a trainee. Only measure low-voltage DC outputs.
Check the meter is set to the right mode before touching anything. Measuring voltage in resistance or current mode can damage the meter.
Never short a power supply's pins with a paperclip or wire to test it. Use a PSU tester.

steps.title: Know the meter
steps.body:
- **Black probe** always goes in **COM**.
- **Red probe** goes in the **VΩ** socket for voltage, resistance and continuity (not the A/mA current sockets).
- **DC voltage** is marked **V⎓** (a straight and dashed line). **AC voltage** is V~.
- **Continuity** is the symbol that looks like a speaker or sound waves: the meter beeps when there is a connection.

steps.title: Measure a CMOS battery
steps.body:
1. Set the meter to **DC voltage**, the 20 V range if it is not auto-ranging.
2. Touch the red probe to the battery's **+** side (the flat side with the writing) and the black probe to the **−** side.
3. A new CR2032 reads about **3.0–3.3 V**.

Below about **2.8 V** it is getting weak. A weak CMOS battery makes the computer lose its date, time and BIOS settings when unplugged.

steps.title: Test continuity
steps.body:
With the cable **disconnected from everything**, set the meter to continuity and touch the probes to the two ends of the same wire. A beep means the wire is unbroken. No beep: the wire is broken or not connected.

This is how you find a broken wire in a cable.

steps.title: Check a PSU with a PSU tester
steps.body:
1. With the PSU **switched off and unplugged**, connect its 24-pin cable (and others) to the tester.
2. Plug in and switch on the PSU.
3. Read each voltage on the tester's display.

ATX power supplies must stay within **±5%** on the main outputs:

| Output | Acceptable range |
|---|---|
| +12 V | 11.40–12.60 V |
| +5 V | 4.75–5.25 V |
| +3.3 V | 3.14–3.47 V |

Any reading outside the range, or a missing output, means the PSU should be replaced.

steps.title: Know the wire colours
steps.body:
Standard ATX wire colours:

- **Yellow:** +12 V
- **Red:** +5 V
- **Orange:** +3.3 V
- **Black:** ground
- **Purple:** +5 V standby (powered whenever the PSU is plugged in and switched on)
- **Green:** PS_ON (turns the PSU on)
- **Grey:** Power Good

The purple standby line is why the motherboard has power even when the computer is "off".

expectedResults: You can measure DC voltage and continuity with the correct meter settings.
You can say whether a CMOS battery or a PSU reading is acceptable.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaving the red probe in the current (A) socket.
commonMistakes.why: Measuring voltage there short-circuits through the meter and can blow its fuse or damage what you are testing.
commonMistakes.fix: Use the VΩ socket for voltage, and check the dial before measuring.

commonMistakes.mistake: Testing continuity on a powered circuit.
commonMistakes.why: Continuity mode sends its own small current; a powered circuit can damage the meter and give false readings.

commonMistakes.mistake: Judging a PSU only by "the fan spins".
commonMistakes.why: A fan can spin while a voltage is out of tolerance, causing random crashes.
commonMistakes.fix: Measure each output against the ±5% range.
